 SOAH DOCKET NUMBER 473-26-16349
PUC DOCKET NUMBER 59475
§
JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC
AND LCRA TRANSMISSION SERVICES CORPORATION TO AMEND THEIR
CERTIFICATES OF CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY FOR THE BELL COUNTY
EAST SWITCH TO BIG HILL SUBSTATION 765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE
PROJECT IN BELL, BURNET, CONCHO, CORYELL, LAMPASAS, LLANO,
MASON, MCCULLOCH, MENARD, MILAM, MILLS, SAN SABA, SCHLEICHER,
TOM GREEN, AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES
§
BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
INITIAL CLOSING BRIEF OF JOE BURNETT AND MICHELLE BURNETT
TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
I. INTRODUCTION AND REQUESTED RELIEF
Joe Burnett and Michelle Burnett ("the Burnetts"), pro se intervenors and directly affected landowners in Bell County, Texas, respectfully submit this Initial Closing Brief in the above-referenced proceeding. We are a married couple who operate a multi-generational farming and ranching business in accordance with local community standards, while also serving in the community banking industry with a combined 65 years of service. Our agricultural operations span multiple units across two Texas counties and represent five generations of production agriculture dating to the late 1800s. We reside at 10335 Sam Neil Lane, Salado, Texas 76571, and our property includes Parcels 3502, 3503, 3504, and 3505, encompassing approximately three-quarters of a mile of Highway 190. [Joe and Michelle Burnett Direct Testimony at 4-5.]
We filed a Motion to Intervene and submitted sworn Direct Testimony, Item 4405, on May 13, 2026, in which we detailed the specific and substantial adverse impacts that any route utilizing Segment/Link A2 would impose on our ranching operations, family property, and future plans. We expressly oppose Segment/Link A2. We support the selection of routes utilizing Segment/Link A3 for the eastern opening of the proposed Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV Transmission Line Project (the "Project") and will support why those Routes are superior with record evidence. [Joe and Michelle Burnett Direct Testimony at 5, 8-9.]
We are aligned with the A2 Segment Affected Landowners Coalition to the extent its position is consistent with ours. This separate brief is offered to emphasize record evidence particularly relevant to our circumstances, including the quantifiable removal of existing solar generation facilities that would result from Segment A2,  the interference with working ranch operations and future rural economic development,, the engineering inefficiencies associated with A2, and the availability of reasonable filed alternatives that utilize A3 while satisfying the Commission's holistic routing criteria. We reserve the right to file reply briefs or additional materials as permitted.
Requested Relief. We respectfully request that the Administrative Law Judges recommend that the Public Utility Commission of Texas ("Commission") approve no route utilizing Segment/Link A2. If the Commission determines that a CCN should issue for the Project, it should select Route 1245, or another reasonable filed route that utilizes Segment A3 for the eastern opening, such as Route 705 as a clean substitute for Route 296, Route 659 as a practical alternative to Route 894, or Route 836 as the closest non-A2 substitute for Route 487or Route 589 as the most comparable A3-based substitute for Route 392.  The Commission should select a route that, when all statutory factors are considered in their totality, better moderates impacts on affected communities and landowners in accordance with PURA § 37.056 and 16 TAC § 25.101.
II. SUMMARY OF POSITION
The record in this proceeding demonstrates that Segment A2 would impose concentrated, avoidable, and disproportionate adverse impacts on an established rural residential and agricultural community in eastern Bell County. These impacts include proximity to occupied habitable structures, interference with active multi-generational cattle ranching operations, including rotational grazing systems and hot-wire fencing, degradation of spring-fed water resources critical for livestock, burdening of prime Highway 190 frontage with future rural economic development potential, including a planned mixed-animal veterinary clinic, and the permanent removal of more than six acres of existing solar generation facilities.  
Segment A3, by contrast, was specifically routed around existing solar facilities and modified after public meetings to increase distances from habitable structures where Applicants had the opportunity to do so. [Tr. Vol. 3 at 239:6-240:4.] That record evidence supports the use of an A3-based route. A3 is not perfect, and we do not contend that any route is without impact. But the record shows that A3-based filed routes exist, and that A2 is not required for a reasonable project.
The filed route set contains multiple reasonable alternatives that utilize the A3 eastern opening (A0-A1-A3) and then follow logical alignments comparable to the routes receiving the most attention, including Routes 894, 487, 392, 296, and others. These alternatives, particularly Routes 1245, 659, 705, 706, 589, and 836, demonstrate that the Commission can approve the Project if it finds need has been established while still avoiding the concentrated and avoidable harms caused by A2.
III. LEGAL STANDARDS GOVERNING ROUTE SELECTION
The Commission's decision on route selection is governed by PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B). Under those standards, the Commission must consider the adequacy of existing service, the need for additional service, the effect on utility serving the area, community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and the probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to consumers in the area.
Section 25.101(b)(3)(B) specifically requires a transmission line to be routed to the extent reasonable, to moderate the impact on the affected communities and landowners unless grid reliability and security dictate otherwise. 
The rule also requires consideration of whether routes use or parallel existing compatible rights-of-way, whether routes parallel property lines or other natural or cultural features, and whether routes conform with the policy of prudent avoidance.

The Applicants’ witnesses confirmed that these factors must be considered holistically. A route paralleling existing roads, pipelines, or property boundaries is a factor the Commission considers, and fewer habitable structures is an indicator of prudent avoidance, even if no single factor controls the final result. [Tr. Vol. 2 at 287:7-288:3.] That is the correct framework here. A2 should not be selected merely because it appears in many route combinations or because it is one way to leave the Bell County East Switch. The question is whether the route moderates impacts on affected landowners and communities to the extent reasonable. On this record, A2 does not.
IV. THE RECORD DEMONSTRATES THAT ROUTES UTILIZING SEGMENT A2 FAIL TO SATISFY THE ROUTING CRITERIA
Segment A2 would place a new 765-kV corridor through an established rural ranching and residential community rather than through empty pasture. It does not simply cross land. It cuts through how land is used, planned, fenced, grazed, accessed, and passed down. 

Our own testimony explains that A2 crosses our parcels diagonally with no regard to property lines, and that the ability to operate temporary hot-wire fencing consistent with historical practices will be hampered if not prohibited from being effective. [Joe and Michelle Burnett Direct Testimony at 12.] Bruce Burnett testified that A2 would dissect his two parcels, create an unwelcome fencing issue for rotational grazing, and drastically change or hinder the family farm and ranch operation. [Bruce Burnett Direct Testimony at 4-5.] Rebecca Burnett testified that A2 would split their best pastures, affect the dry cabin, steel working pens, underground waterlines, permanent cross fences, temporary cross fences, crop production, cattle, hay production, and grazing lands. [Rebecca Burnett Direct Testimony at 5-6.]

A. A2 Results in Concentrated Proximity to Habitable Structures and Fails Prudent Avoidance
The record contains detailed, sworn testimony from numerous landowners along the A2 corridor documenting occupied, full-time residences near or directly affected by the proposed centerline. 


Examples include:
Donna Anne Kelln – home approximately 275 feet from centerline (easement ~175 feet from residence); property includes pool, gardens, animal-care areas, and family burial sites. [Donna Anne Kelln Direct Testimony at 8-9, 17-18.]
Sherry Moore – A2 approximately 159 feet from home and 219 feet from shed; and raises drainage and soil disturbance concerns.  [Sherry Moore Direct Testimony at 4, 6, 8.]
Brandon Fortie – full-time occupied rural homestead approximately 282 feet from A2; cattle use areas and agricultural space with no existing right-of-way on the property. [Brandon Fortie Direct Testimony at 5-6, 10-12.]
Bradley and Angela Woolard – A2 approximately 250 feet from their daughter's residence; crosses central portion of property and planned future retirement home location. [Bradley and Angela Woolard Direct Testimony at 6-7, 12-13, 17-19.]
Kasey Woolard – A2 approximately 250 feet from residence and septic system; divides central usable portion of property intended for future family residence. [Kasey Woolard Direct Testimony at 6, 8-11, 18-19.]
Additional testimony from Aaron and Alison Bechter, Jennifer Adams, Raymond and Tracy Balderas, Cory and Gretta Boston, Clifford Dyer, William Hurst, Monroe Jimenez, Ronald and Teresa Jurca, Jeff Kirby, Lindsey and Randall Marek, Billy and Sherrie Potter, Romeo Trevino, Kenny Ware, and others describes active rural residential and agricultural use immediately adjacent to or crossed by A2, with many homes and structures outside the strict 500-foot metric but still experiencing profound land-use, community, and quality-of-life impacts. [A2 Segment Affected Landowners Coalition Direct Testimony at 4-7, 9-11.]
This is not just a habitable-structure count. It is a concentrated land-use impact on a working rural community. Still, the habitable-structure evidence also matters. A3 was modified after public meetings where Applicants had the opportunity to move it farther from habitable structures. Mr. Marusak testified that “every little bit helps” and that the A3 modification was made to address landowner concerns from a meeting. [Tr. Vol. 3 at 239:18-240:4.] That testimony confirms that the Applicants understood the importance of moving lines away from homes and property uses when the routing record allowed it.

Joe and Michelle also testified that, according to the route data available to them, 942 of the 1,246 route IDs include Segment A2, while 217 include Segment A3. [Joe and Michelle Burnett Direct Testimony at 8.] That number matters because it shows the degree to which A2 dominates the filed route universe. But the Commission is not required to select a route merely because A2 appears repeatedly in the route set. The Commission must choose a route that best satisfies the routing criteria as a whole.

B. A2 Would Permanently Remove Existing Solar Generation Facilities, A Quantifiable and Avoidable Impact
One of the most concrete and measurable distinctions between A2 and A3 is the impact on existing solar generation. This issue was developed through cross-examination and is not speculative.
Mr. Marusak testified that solar generation facilities are located within the study area in Bell, Coryell, and Menard Counties. When asked whether that count had decreased since the 2023 reference, he testified, “It certainly would not go down. I can’t imagine them ripping them out.” [Tr. Vol. 3 at 237:8-15.] He then confirmed that solar farms are common and expansive near the Bell County East Switch. [Tr. Vol. 3 at 237:19-238:3.]
That testimony matters because A2 would do exactly what Mr. Marusak said he could not imagine generally happening. It would rip out existing solar generation. When asked about A2’s approximately 1,400-foot crossing through a 200-foot right-of-way, Mr. Marusak agreed that the crossing would remove more than six acres of solar farm. Applicants further acknowledged that they had not calculated the amount of electric generating capacity that would be permanently removed if Link A2 were constructed. [Tr. Vol. 3 at 238:9-239:5.]
Mr. Marusak then confirmed that Link A3 was routed to go around the solar farm facilities as an alternative. [Tr. Vol. 3 at 239:6-11.] He also testified that A3 was later amended, where Applicants had the opportunity to increase distance from habitable structures and address landowner concerns raised at a public meeting. [Tr. Vol. 3 at 239:13-240:4.]
This is not a generalized landowner preference. It is a known, measurable, and avoidable impact to existing Texas energy infrastructure. Applicants are asking the Commission to approve a 765-kV transmission line while proposing an A2 alignment that would remove existing solar generation, without calculating the MW loss, even though a filed alternative, A3, was routed around those same solar facilities.
The record also shows why this matters in the broader need discussion. Mr. Martin testified that Applicants do not build generation, that generation is generally handled by the private sector, and that Applicants work with generators through the interconnection process in an open-access system. [Tr. Vol. 4 at 43:1-12.] If generation is left to the private sector, the Commission should not casually approve a route that destroys existing private generation when a filed alternative avoids that loss. On this record, the solar-generation impact weighs heavily against any route utilizing A2.
C. A2 Burdens Highway 190 Frontage, Interferes with Established Ranch Operations, and Degrades Critical Water Resources
Our Direct Testimony and the testimony of neighboring landowners detail the profound interference A2 would cause with active agricultural operations,  rural land use, water resources, and future family development. 
Our property is used today for cattle production and recreation, including rotational grazing supported by temporary hot-wire fencing systems. Segment A2 would diagonally cross multiple parcels, fragmenting the property, interfering with fencing alignment, restricting full use of pastures, and burdening prime Highway 190 frontage that has rural commercial and economic development value consistent with the rural character of the area. [Joe and Michelle Burnett Direct Testimony at 5, 9-12; Joe and Michelle Burnett Exs. 2 and 3.]
Our daughter, Brooke Burnett, a pre-veterinary student, intends to establish a mixed-animal veterinary clinic on the family Highway 190 property. This future use is not speculative; it is a concrete plan for rural economic development that would serve the local agricultural community. A2 would limit where such a facility could be located. Highway frontage access is highly favorable for such uses, yet Applicants' land-use evaluation focused primarily on existing rather than future development potential. An A3-based eastern opening avoids the Burnett-specific A2 conflicts documented in this record. [Joe and Michelle Burnett Direct Testimony at 12; Brooke Burnett Direct Testimony at 4, 6-7; Tr. Vol. 3 at 243:19-245:2.]
The A2 corridor also contains documented spring-fed water resources critical to livestock operations, particularly during drought conditions. Romeo Trevino testified that his spring-fed stock tank is approximately 154 feet from the proposed centerline and can be the last natural water source for livestock on contiguous properties during severe drought. Monroe Jimenez described a spring-fed creek and a spring-fed pond less than 10 feet east of the proposed line. William Hurst described a natural spring-fed stock tank and recurring flooding/drainage concerns. These are not ordinary stream crossings. They are interconnected rural water systems supporting working agricultural land. The Combined Data Table's stream-crossing counts do not capture the full scope of these site-specific impacts. [Romeo Trevino Direct Testimony at 13; Monroe Jimenez Direct Testimony at 8-10; William Hurst Direct Testimony at 14-16.]
Additional testimony from Bruce Burnett, Rebecca Burnett, and others describes impacts on ranch roads, waterlines, working pens, creek crossings (including Glass Branch wildlife movement), EMS/fire access, and next-generation family use of the land.  A3-based routes avoid the A2 impacts documented in this section.  [Bruce Burnett Direct Testimony at 6-9, 17-18; Rebecca Burnett Direct Testimony at 5-8.]
D. A2 Introduces Unnecessary Engineering Inefficiencies and Cost Variables
Engineering testimony also weighs against treating A2 as a simple or harmless route choice. Ms. Cooley testified that any 90-degree turn requires a full-tension dead-end structure. [Tr. Vol. 2 at 195:22-196:7.] She also testified that a full-tension dead-end structure requires more steel than a tangent structure, and that in most cases there is a percent increase in steel compared with a tangent structure. [Tr. Vol. 4 at 58:23-59:16.]
Staff witness John Poole agreed that turning structures are a significant cost variable and that each additional route turn increases cost because turning structures are materially different from tangent structures. He also agreed that his cost attachment broke costs into right-of-way, engineering, procurement, and construction, but did not separately identify structure types or dead-end structures. [Tr. Vol. 4 at 207:14-208:20.] 
The A3 eastern opening does not require the same 90-degree turn at the Bell County East Switch opening. While cost is one factor among many, the record shows that A2's engineering inefficiencies are avoidable through selection of an A3-based route without disproportionate penalty to overall project economics.
V. REASONABLE FILED NON-A2 ALTERNATIVES EXIST AND BETTER SATISFY THE ROUTING CRITERIA
The Coalition's Initial Post-Hearing Brief correctly identifies multiple filed routes that utilize the A3 eastern opening and demonstrate that A2 is not necessary. We highlight the following as particularly relevant to the routes receiving the most attention in this proceeding:
Route 1245: The strongest overall non-A2 alternative in the filed route set. It avoids A2 entirely and is approximately 216.79 miles in length with an estimated transmission-line cost of approximately $1.659 billion, shorter and less expensive than Routes 487, 296, and 894 (all of which utilize A2). [Applicants Ex. 1, App. D, Attachment B, Combined Data Table.]
Route 659: A practical and strong substitute for Route 894. It avoids A2, has 93 habitable structures (only eight more than Route 894), fewer stream crossings than Route 894, and the same number of cultural resources within 1,000 feet. [Applicants Ex. 1, App. D, Attachment B, Combined Data Table.]
Route 705: The cleanest A3 substitution for Route 296. It replaces Route 296's A0-A1-A2-B1-C2 eastern opening with A0-A1-A3-A6-C1, then follows the same general route as Route 296 from D11 through Z2. This demonstrates that the A3 opening can be substituted while preserving the overall route concept. Route 706 is a similar, slightly less expensive option. [Applicants Ex. 1, App. D, Attachment B, Combined Data Table; Brandon Fortie Direct Testimony (Interchange Item 4807) supporting A3, A6, and C1 for reduced impact to occupied residences and greater paralleling of existing corridors.]
Route 589: The closest filed non-A2 substitute for Route 392. It successfully replaces Route 392's A0-A1-A2-B1-C2 eastern opening with the less impactful A0-A1-A3-A6-C1 alignment. By doing so, it preserves the general trajectory of Route 392 across the remainder of the project area without relying on the highly disruptive A2 segment. [Applicants Ex. 1, App. D, Attachment B, Combined Data Table.]
Route 836: The closest non-A2 substitute for Route 487. It avoids A2 while preserving much of Route 487's route structure after F1. [Applicants Ex. 1, App. D, Attachment B, Combined Data Table.]
These alternatives are not theoretical; they are fully filed routes supported by the same Combined Data Table and Environmental Assessment that underpin the Applicants' preferred routing. They show that the Commission can approve the Project, if it determines need is satisfied,  while selecting a route that utilizes A3, moderates impacts on the eastern Bell County community, avoids destruction of existing solar generation, and satisfies the paralleling and prudent avoidance preferences that have historically carried significant weight in Commission decisions. The Commission has the discretion, and the statutory responsibility, to make that choice.
VI. CONCLUSION AND PRAYER
For the reasons stated above, Joe Burnett and Michelle Burnett respectfully request that the Administrative Law Judges recommend that the Public Utility Commission of Texas:
Deny or defer the application to the extent the Commission finds the record insufficient on need or less intrusive alternatives.; or
If the Commission grants a CCN, approve no route using Segment/Link A2 and instead select Route 1245 or another reasonable filed route that utilizes Segment A3 for the eastern opening, such as Routes 589,  659, 705, 706, or 836, or any other route that, when all factors under PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) are considered in their totality, best moderates impacts on affected communities and landowners while serving the public interest in reliable electric service.
A decision selecting an A3-based route would represent a balanced, record-supported outcome that respects the statutory mandate to moderate impacts on rural communities and landowners, preserves existing renewable solar-generation facilities shown in the record, avoids concentrating new corridor burdens on an established rural ranching and residential community, respects future rural economic development along Highway 190, and reflects holistic consideration of all routing criteria. Such a decision would serve the public interest while avoiding the specific, record-supported harms caused by Segment A2. 

We appreciate the opportunity to participate in this proceeding and the careful attention of the Administrative Law Judges and Commission Staff to the full record. We reserve the right to file reply briefing as permitted.

Respectfully submitted,

and Avoidable Impact

One ofthe most concrete and measurable distinctions between A2 and A3 is the impact on
existing solar generation. This issue was developed through cross-examination and is not
speculative.

Mr. Marusak testified that solar generation facilities are located within the study area in Bell,
Coryell, and Menard Counties. When asked whether that count had decreased since the 2023
reference, he testified, "It certainly would not go down. I can't imagine them ripping them out."
[Tr. Vol. 3 at 237:8-15.] He then confirmed that solar farms are common and expansive near the
Bell County East Switch. [Tr. Vol. 3 at 237:19-238:3.]

That testimony matters because A2 would do exactly what Mr. Marusak said he could not
imagine generally happening. It would rip out existing solar generation. When asked about A2's
approximately 1,400-foot crossing through a 200-foot right-of-way, Mr. Marusak agreed that the
crossing would remove more than six acres of solar farm. Applicants further acknowledged that
they had not calculated the amount of electric generating capacity that would be permanently
removed if Link A2 were constructed. [Tr. Vol. 3 at 238:9-239:5.I

Mr. Marusak then confirmed that Link A3 was routed to go around the solar farm facilities as an
alternative. [Tr. Vol. 3 at 239:6-11.] He also testified that A3 was later amended, where
Applicants had the opportunity to increase distance from habitable structures and address
landowner concerns raised at a public meeting. [Tr. Vol. 3 at 239:13-240:4.]

This is not a generalized landowner preference. It is a known, measurable, and avoidable impact
to existing Texas energy infrastructure. Applicants are asking the Commission to approve a 765-
kV transmission line while proposing an A2 alignment that would remove existing solar
generation, without calculating the MW loss, even though a filed alternative, A3, was routed
around those same solar facilities.

The record also shows why this matters in the broader need discussion. Mr. Martin testified that
Applicants do not build generation, that generation is generally handled by the private sector, and
that Applicants work with generators through the interconnection process in an open-access
system. [Tr. Vol. 4 at 43:1-12.I If generation is left to the private sector, the Commission should
not casually approve a route that destroys existing private generation when a filed alternative
avoids that loss. On this record, the solar-generation impact weighs heavily against any route
utilizing A2.

D. A2 Introduces Unnecessary Engineering Inefficiencies and Cost Variables
Engineering testimony also weighs against treating A2 as a simple or harmless route choice. Ms.
Cooley testified that any 90-degree turn requires a full-tension dead-end structure. [Tr. Vol. 2 at
195:22-196:7.] She also testified that a full-tension dead-end structure requires more steel than a
tangent structure, and that in most cases there is a percent increase in steel compared with a
tangent structure. [Tr. Vol. 4 at 58:23-59:16.]

Staff witness John Poole agreed that turning structures are a significant cost variable and that
each additional route turn increases cost because turning structures are materially different from
tangent structures. He also agreed that his cost attachment broke costs into right-of-way,
engineering, procurement, and construction, but did not separately identify structure types or
dead-end structures. [Tr. Vol. 4 at 207:14-208:20.]

The A3 eastern opening does not require the same 90-degree turn at the Bell County East Switch
opening. While cost is one factor among many, the record shows that A2's engineering
inefficiencies are avoidable through selection of an A3-based route without disproportionate
penalty to overall project economics.
